items.prose: A desk logs 400 trading days of one stock. It opened with a price gap on 120 days and closed up on 260 days. On 78 days it did both.

parts.question: What is $P(\text{up} \mid \text{gap})$ in this sample? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the up closes inside the 120 gap days.

byKey.over-all: You divided by all 400 days. That is $P(\text{up} \cap \text{gap})$.
byKey.reversed: You divided by the 260 up days. That is $P(\text{gap} \mid \text{up})$.

explain.text: Of the 120 gap days, 78 closed up. So $P(\text{up} \mid \text{gap}) = \tfrac{78}{120} = 0.65$.

parts.question: Using 0.65 from part 1, is an up close independent of a gap in this sample?

options.text: No: 78 days had both, so the two are linked
options.why: Sharing days is not dependence. Compare $P(\text{up} \mid \text{gap})$ with $P(\text{up})$.
That compares a joint chance with a single one. The product test uses $0.3 \times 0.65 = 0.195$, which matches.

options.text: Yes, because the two events never overlap
options.why: They overlap on 78 days. Two events with positive chances that never overlap are dependent.

feedback.correct: A gap leaves the chance of an up close at 0.65, so the two are independent here.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the chance of an up close given a gap with the chance over all days.

explain.text: Over all days $P(\text{up}) = \tfrac{260}{400} = 0.65$, the same as given a gap. Equivalently $\tfrac{120}{400} \times 0.65 = 0.195 = \tfrac{78}{400}$, so the product test passes.

parts.question: Treat gap days as independent trials, each closing up with chance 0.65. Over the next 4 gap days, what is the chance of exactly 3 up closes? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find one path's chance, then count the paths with exactly 3 up closes.

byKey.one-path: That is one order only. The down day can fall on any of the 4 days.
byKey.all-four: That is the chance all 4 close up. Exactly 3 needs one down day.
byKey.joint-slip: You used 0.195, the joint chance, as the up rate. Each gap day closes up with chance 0.65.

explain.text: One path, such as up, up, up, down, has chance $0.65^3 \times 0.35 \approx 0.09612$. The down day can be any of 4, so the chance is $4 \times 0.09612 \approx 0.3845$.

parts.question: Using the same 0.65, what is the chance at least one of the next 4 gap days closes down? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance that none closes down, then take it from 1.

byKey.sum: You added 0.35 four times. The days can overlap, so use the complement.
byKey.exactly-one: That is exactly one down close. Two, three or four down closes count too.
byKey.all-down: That is the chance all 4 close down. At least one needs only one.

explain.text: No down close means 4 up closes, with chance $0.65^4 \approx 0.1785$. So at least one down close has chance $1 - 0.1785 \approx 0.8215$.

items.prose: A strategy has a losing week if its signal fails, or a liquidity squeeze hits, or both. In a given week the signal fails with chance 0.3 and a squeeze hits with chance 0.25, independently.

parts.question: What is the chance of a losing week? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A week is safe only if neither cause happens.

byKey.sum: You added 0.3 and 0.25. That counts the weeks with both causes twice.
byKey.both: That is the chance both causes hit. Either one is enough for a loss.

explain.text: A safe week needs no failure and no squeeze, with chance $0.7 \times 0.75 = 0.525$. So a losing week has chance $1 - 0.525 = 0.475$.

parts.question: Using 0.475 from part 1, the week was a loss. What is the chance the signal failed? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A failed signal always means a loss. Divide its chance by the chance of a loss.

byKey.no-news: That is the chance before you knew of the loss. The loss raises it.
byKey.sum-slip: You divided by 0.55 from part 1's slip. The chance of a loss is 0.475.
byKey.times: You multiplied 0.3 by 0.475. Divide by the chance of the news instead.

explain.text: A failed signal always brings a loss, so $P(\text{fail} \cap \text{loss}) = 0.3$. Dividing by 0.475 gives $P(\text{fail} \mid \text{loss}) \approx 0.6316$.

parts.question: You then learn a squeeze did hit that week. What is the chance the signal failed now? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The squeeze explains the loss alone, so the signal is back to its own 0.3.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A squeeze always brings a loss, so the loss now tells you nothing more about the signal.

byKey.still: That was the chance before you heard of the squeeze. The squeeze explains the loss.
byKey.cancelled: The squeeze explains the loss, but the signal can still have failed as well.
byKey.over-loss: You divided 0.075, both causes, by 0.475. The news is now the squeeze, with chance 0.25.

explain.text: A squeeze means a loss whatever the signal did, so the loss adds nothing. The causes are independent, so $P(\text{fail} \mid \text{squeeze}) = 0.3$.

parts.question: Using parts 2 and 3: given a loss, are a failed signal and a squeeze independent?

options.text: No: the squeeze moved the chance of a failure from 0.63 to 0.3
Yes: they were independent before the loss, so they still are
options.why: Independence before is not independence given a shared effect. The squeeze moved the chance from 0.63 to 0.3.

options.text: Yes: the squeeze left the chance at the 0.3 it started at
options.why: Compare with 0.63, the chance given the loss alone. The squeeze moved it down.

options.text: No: given a loss, at most one of the two can have happened
options.why: A week with both still counts as a loss, so both can happen.

feedback.correct: Given the loss, news of a squeeze lowered the chance of a failed signal.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the chance of a failure given the loss with the chance given the loss and the squeeze.

explain.text: Given the loss, the failure has chance 0.632, but adding the squeeze drops it to 0.3. Conditioning on a shared effect makes independent causes dependent.

items.prose: A small book holds three loans. In a recession year, which comes with chance 0.25, each loan defaults with chance 0.28. In a normal year each defaults with chance 0.04. Given the year's type, the loans default independently.

parts.question: What is the overall chance that one given loan defaults? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each regime's default chance by the chance of that regime.

byKey.average: You averaged 0.28 and 0.04 equally. Normal times are three times as likely as a recession.
byKey.recession-only: That is the recession path alone. Add the normal path, $0.75 \times 0.04$.

explain.text: The recession path gives $0.25 \times 0.28 = 0.07$ and the normal path $0.75 \times 0.04 = 0.03$. Together one loan defaults with chance $0.1$.

parts.question: What is the chance all three loans default? Give a decimal to four significant figures.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Inside each regime the three defaults are independent, so cube that regime's chance. Then weight and add.

byKey.independent: You cubed the overall 0.1. The loans are independent only inside each regime.
byKey.no-weights: You added the two regime chances without weighting them by 0.25 and 0.75.
byKey.cube-average: You cubed the average of the two regime chances, 0.16. Cube inside each regime, then weight.

explain.text: In a recession all three default with chance $0.28^3 = 0.021952$, and in normal times $0.04^3 = 0.000064$. Weighting by 0.25 and 0.75 gives $0.005488 + 0.000048 = 0.005536$.

parts.question: A model takes the overall chance of 0.1 from part 1 and treats the loans as independent. What does it give for all three defaulting? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Independent defaults multiply: one factor of 0.1 per loan.

byKey.sum: You added 0.1 three times. All three defaulting needs a product.
byKey.squared: That is two loans. The book holds three, so cube 0.1.

explain.text: Treated as independent, each loan contributes a factor of 0.1. So the model gives $0.1^3 = 0.001$.

parts.question: Part 2 gave 0.005536 and part 3 gave 0.001. How many times the model's chance is the true chance? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{0.005536}{0.001} = 5.536$: the shared economy makes a wipe-out over five times as likely.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the true chance by the model's chance.

byKey.reciprocal: You divided the model's chance by the true one. Put the true chance on top.
byKey.difference: That is the difference. The question asks how many times as large.
byKey.weights-slip: You used 0.022, part 2's unweighted slip. The true chance is 0.005536.

explain.text: The ratio is $\tfrac{0.005536}{0.001} = 5.536$. The shared recession makes the loans fail together. So the model understates the worst case more than five times over.

items.prose: A firm has three desks, and each pair of desks shares one price feed: feed $P$ is read by desks 1 and 2, feed $Q$ by desks 1 and 3, and feed $R$ by desks 2 and 3. Each day every feed independently shows up or down, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. A desk is calm on a day when its two feeds agree. Let $A$ be “desk 1 is calm”, $B$ be “desk 2 is calm” and $C$ be “desk 3 is calm”. Each has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

parts.question: What is $P(C \mid A)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: Given $A$, feeds $P$ and $Q$ agree. Desk 3 is calm exactly when $R$ matches them, which has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Fix feeds $P$ and $Q$ as agreeing and ask what $R$ needs for desk 3 to be calm.

byKey.certain: Desk 1 being calm does not make desk 3 calm. Feed $R$ is still free to differ from $Q$.

explain.text: Given $A$, feeds $P$ and $Q$ agree. Desk 3 is calm only if $R$ matches them, one of its 2 equally likely values, so $P(C \mid A) = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

parts.question: Using part 1, and the same argument for the other pairs, which statement is true?

options.text: Each pair of $A$, $B$ and $C$ is independent
$A$ and $C$ are dependent, since desks 1 and 3 share feed $Q$
options.why: The desks do share $Q$, but learning $A$ left the chance of $C$ at $\tfrac{1}{2}$. That is the test.

options.text: Only $A$ and $B$ are independent, as they are desks 1 and 2
options.why: Run the test on $A$ and $C$: $P(C \mid A) = \tfrac{1}{2} = P(C)$. That pair passes too.

options.text: No pair is independent, as every pair of desks shares a feed
options.why: Sharing a feed is not dependence. Each pair passes the test, as part 1 showed for $A$ and $C$.

feedback.correct: Every pair passes: learning one desk is calm leaves another at $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Run the test $P(C \mid A) = P(C)$ on each pair.

explain.text: Part 1 gave $P(C \mid A) = \tfrac{1}{2} = P(C)$. The same argument works for each other pair of desks, so all three pairs are independent.

parts.question: What is $P(A \cap B \cap C)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: If desks 1 and 2 are calm, $P = Q = R$, so desk 3 is calm too. So $P = P(A \cap B) = \tfrac{1}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. If desks 1 and 2 are both calm, what do you know about all three feeds?

byKey.product: You multiplied three halves, as if the events were mutually independent. Pairwise independence does not give that.
byKey.single: That is $P(C)$ alone. Desks 1 and 2 must be calm too, which already settles $C$.

explain.text: Desks 1 and 2 both calm means $P = Q = R$, which already makes desk 3 calm. So $A \cap B$ lies inside $C$, and $P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A \cap B) = \tfrac{2}{8} = \tfrac{1}{4}$, not $\tfrac{1}{8}$.

parts.question: Using part 3, what is $P(C \mid A \cap B)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{1/4}{1/4} = 1$: two calm desks make the third calm every time.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide part 3 by $P(A \cap B)$.

byKey.pairwise: That treats $A$ and $B$ together as no news, like each alone. Together they fix $C$.
byKey.joint: That is part 3's joint chance. Divide it by $P(A \cap B) = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

explain.text: $P(C \mid A \cap B) = \tfrac{P(A \cap B \cap C)}{P(A \cap B)} = \tfrac{1/4}{1/4} = 1$. Each pair told you nothing, but $A$ and $B$ together settle $C$.

parts.question: Watch the desks on 8 independent days. Using part 3, what is the chance at least one day has $A$, $B$ and $C$ all happening? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance no day has all three, then take it from 1.

byKey.product-slip: You used $\tfrac{1}{8}$ a day, from the mutual-independence slip in part 3. The true chance is $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
byKey.sum: You added $\tfrac{1}{4}$ eight times. Days can both hit, so use the complement.
byKey.complement: That is the chance no day has all three. Take it from 1.

explain.text: A day misses the triple with chance $1 - \tfrac{1}{4} = 0.75$. All 8 miss with chance $0.75^8 \approx 0.1001$, so at least one hit has chance $\approx 0.8999$.
